content.overview: BNS s. 73 — Printing or publishing any matter relating to Court proceedings without permission.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Printing or publishing any matter relating to Court proceedings without permission. BNS restatement of IPC 228A (publication). Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 228A (publication). Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 73 is the rule on “Printing or publishing any matter relating to Court proceedings without permission”. The section provides that whoever prints or publishes any matter in relation to any proceeding before a Court with respect to an offence referred to in section 72 without the previous permission of such Court shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years and shall also be liable to fine. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 73 exists so that “Printing or publishing any matter relating to Court proceedings without permission” has a closed legal test in Chapter V — Of Offences Against Woman and Child. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: Sexual offences, assault, marriage, miscarriage, and offences against the child — placed first among the offence chapters.

The provision in detail
73. Whoever prints or publishes any matter in relation to any proceeding before a Court with respect to an offence referred to in section 72 without the previous permission of such Court shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years and shall also be liable to fine

Essential ingredients
1. Whoever prints or publishes any matter in relation to any proceeding before a Court with respect to an offence referred to in section 72 without the previous permission of such Court shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years and shall also be liable to fine

Explanations
Explanation.—The printing or publication of the judgment of any High Court or the Supreme Court does not amount to an offence within the meaning of this section

learningObjectives: Understand the prohibition against unauthorized publication of in camera court proceedings under BNS s. 73.
Examine the requirement of prior permission of the court.
State the punishment: imprisonment up to two years and fine.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 73 provides that whoever prints or publishes any matter in relation to any proceeding, that has been conducted in camera, before a court with respect to an offence referred to in sub-section (1) of section 72, without the previous permission of such court, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years and shall also be liable to fine.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Trials of sexual offences are conducted in camera to provide a safe, fearless environment for survivor testimony. Unauthorized public reporting of sensitive in camera proceedings undermines judicial confidentiality and is penalized with up to two years imprisonment.
statutoryFramework: Chapter V — Of Offences against Women and Children, BNS s. 73 (corresponding to IPC s. 228A(3)).
Prerequisite: Court proceedings conducted in camera under BNSS (e.g. trials of offences under ss. 64 to 71).
Prohibited conduct: Printing or publishing any matter relating to such proceedings.
Exception: Done with 'the previous permission of such court'.
Penalty: Imprisonment up to two years and fine.
essentialIngredients: Court proceedings with respect to sexual offences under ss. 64–71 were conducted in camera.
The accused printed or published reports or matter relating to those proceedings.
The publication was made without previous permission of the court.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Under Section 366 BNSS (formerly CrPC s. 327), trials of rape and sexual offences are mandated to be conducted in camera (in closed court, excluding the public and media). Section 73 reinforces this procedural protection by imposing criminal penalties on any journalist, blogger, or spectator who leaks, prints, or broadcasts testimony, cross-examination transcripts, or proceedings from that closed courtroom without obtaining prior written permission from the presiding judge.
examples: Teaching example (Leaking in camera testimony): A reporter attends a closed-door rape trial and publishes verbatim witness cross-examination in a morning daily without court permission. Section 73 is breached; the reporter faces up to two years imprisonment.

Teaching example (Official court release): A judge grants permission to publish a redacted summary of the legal ruling. Publishing that approved summary does not violate s. 73 because previous permission was granted.
distinctions: In camera proceedings vs Open court reporting: Open court proceedings enjoy qualified press reporting; in camera proceedings are completely closed by law.
Section 72 (Victim identity) vs Section 73 (Court proceedings): Section 72 protects the victim's name; Section 73 protects the integrity of the closed trial proceedings.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether a courtroom observer who live-tweeted confidential testimony from an in camera sexual assault trial can be prosecuted under BNS s. 73.
Rule: Section 73 prohibits publishing any matter relating to in camera proceedings of sexual offences without prior court permission.
Application: The trial was in camera, and live-tweeting constitutes public dissemination without judicial permission.
Conclusion: The observer is guilty under s. 73.
